en: The Book of the Night Attack (Sauptikaparva)
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the best of men, as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī and Vyāsa, one should then utter the word "Victory! (Jayamudīrayet).
When the sun, the abode of majesty and beloved of the lotuses, had set,
the earth became shrouded in darkness, as if its hair were disheveled by grief.
When the day had been brought to an end by time and the sacrificial fires of the twilight had subsided,
the sky became filled with stars as if it were covered with nothing but bones.
Śyāmā, her vision clouded by spreading darkness due to fresh sorrow, bore a shimmering array of star-like teardrops like falling stars.
In that terrible face of night, in the forest dense with fearsome creatures,
Kṛpa and Kṛtavarman fell asleep from exhaustion.
Meditating on the slaughter of Duryodhana and overwhelmed by the *hālāhala* poison of his wrath,
the son of Droṇa alone contemplated his vow for the destruction of the enemy.
In the meantime, he saw a circle of crows perched upon the high summit of a banyan tree, being attacked by an owl.
Seeing the crows that had arrived by the power of Time and been struck down by the owl,
the son of Droṇa reflected upon that very same policy for the slaughter of the Pāṇḍavas.
Having formed a cruel resolve out of anger and having awakened Kṛpa and Bhoja,
he spoke while sighing deeply, as if burning with rage.
The king, who alone stood in a precarious position against thousands of kings,
has been struck down by Bhīmasena through this deceit while we are still alive.
Bearing weapons, we have seen him on the ground in vain,
like utterly impotent men incapable of remedying his fall with even a single tear.
Relying on the right place and time, an enemy must be slain with all one's might;
therefore, I shall slay the Pāṇḍavas along with their followers this very day while they are still asleep.

Hearing this, Kṛpa, his mind shrinking with distress and filled with compassion as he censured the sin of killing one who was fast asleep, spoke to his sister’s son: Bhagavadgītā 11.13.13: śrutvaitatkūṇitamanāḥ prasuptavadhapātakam / kṛpaḥ kṛpākulo nindannabhāṣata sutaṃ svasuḥ // 11.13 // Having heard this, Kṛpa—his mind recoiling at the sin of slaying one who was fast asleep, and overwhelmed by pity—spoke, reproaching his sister's son.
"Shame on this despicable battle where one is slain while motionless!
Even when their fortitude is broken, our illustrious heroes do not strike."
"Your Majesty, I, and Bhoja— let us all act this very morning so that we shall not have to endure again the agony caused by the slaughter of Duryodhana."
United together in battle, we shall be a match even for the gods;
we will enter the forest of our enemies like blazing fires.
When Gautama had spoken thus, and Kṛtavarman had given his consent,
the son of Dṛṇi, sighing with eyes full of tears, spoke again.
Those who move about among the wise with deceit, like a magician,
and touch the boundaries of unrighteousness, do not partake in the fruit thereof.
Karna was slain by Arjuna, as was that son of Śantanu;
how could this not be known in the world? It is impossible to say anything further.
Now, I offer this salutation with joined palms to Dharma for his well-being;
for I cannot endure this defeat that tears at my very vitals.
Having spoken thus with a cruel resolve, the son of Droṇa, firm in his determination,
set out for the Kuru camp in the darkness by means of his chariot.
At the command of Kṛṣṇa, after the Pāṇḍavas had previously departed for their own camp along with Sātyaki and their warriors, they remained there without their followers.
Having overtaken Kṛpa and Bhoja with his speed, the son of Droṇa arrived and,
reaching the gate of the camp, beheld a great being.
With a tawny beard, matted locks, and eyes like a mass of flames,
he resembled a collection of darknesses and was like a mountain of collyrium.
He has a thousand heads and eyes, and a thousand feet—wondrous;
his body is encircled by a serpent as a sacred thread, and he wears serpents as armlets and bracelets;
he is terrifying, like the very deity of Death (Kṛtānta) who brings fear even to fear itself.
Seeing that, the son of Droṇa, whose valor was difficult to overcome and who was a mountain of fortitude, launched a volley of all his weapons at him with terrible fury.
Those weapons, suddenly blazing with splendor,
met their destruction upon encountering that great being as it roared.
Then the son of Droṇa, filled with wonder, beheld from those rays thousands of discus-weaponed forms emerging.
In an instant, his weapon was snatched away by him; tormented by the heat of intense remorse, he, agitated, reproached himself for the foul deed he had committed.
Then, descending from his chariot, he approached the wielder of the trident, the destroyer of Tripura,
with a face made resonant by the recitation of that hymn, standing there with disciplined composure.
When he was prepared to offer himself as a sacrifice to Rudra upon that [altar],
a golden altar filled with flames appeared before him.
With the fierce hosts produced from that [body], which had various animals for their mouths and bellies and were armed with various blazing weapons, he quickly filled the sky.
Then, when the great fire upon the sacrificial altar had blazed up, the son of Droṇa,
offering himself with devotion to the Three-eyed Lord, threw himself into it.
Then the Blessed One, the slayer of Andhaka, having arrived in person, was pleased and said to him:
"Arise, O best of the Aṅgirases; you are my very own portion."
I have performed all this for the sake of the manifestation of the Enemy of Kaiṭabha;
know Kṛṣṇa to be my very self—he is always highly esteemed by me.
"The Pāñcālas are already ripe for their end; there is no protection for them anywhere.
Take this sword and tear them apart without hesitation."
Having spoken thus and given a blazing sword to Bhairava, who then vanished,
the son of Droṇa, difficult to behold due to his transformation, entered the camp.
Having stationed Bhoja and Kṛpa at the gate for the sake of slaying those who had fled,
he entered and beheld Dhṛṣṭadyumna upon a white bed.
With its claws of brilliant pearl necklace-rays, resembling a blazing lion,
it was gazed upon by the lamps with their swirling flames as if out of wonder.
It was occupied by many soldiers who were exhausted from the pressure of numerous battles, overcome by sleep, and who had dismounted from their saddled horses.
Seeing him, the son of Droṇa, burning with the fire of anger and remembering his father, said, "Rise up, you slayer of your guru! and struck him with his foot.
Suddenly awakened by him and seizing his weapons in agitation,
the son of Drupada trembled upon recognizing the son of Droṇa.
The son of Droṇa, seizing him by the hair adorned with garlands as he rose up with speed,
dragged him down and violently throttled him until he was overwhelmed.
Being crushed with fury, his face agitated by the spitting out of blood,
he became enraged and, quivering, struck the elephant’s feet with his claws and teeth.
"Quickly cut me with a weapon, not with your foot! he cried out in a faltering voice; his tone was choked in his throat and his syllables indistinct due to panting.
The son of Droṇa said to him: "O wicked one, you shall be slain by my feet;
for there is no sin in those who kill their preceptors, as they have been purified by weapons in the eyes of the world."
Having said this, he crushed him, who was already shattered by kicks to the feet;
when he was slain, the people woke up from the sound of that commotion.
***** The Slaying of Dhṛṣṭadyumna ***** Then,
beholding the son of Droṇa marked by splashes of the blood of his enemies,
the Pāñcālas and the sons of Draupadī thought, "This is the hour [of our end]. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.48)
As they brought weapons to one another with eyes reddened by the remnants of sleep, and cried out to each other, "Armor!
Armor!", there arose a great clamor from them.
"Where is the elephant? Where is the chariot? Where is the horse? Where is the bow?
Where are the arrows?"—speaking thus, the son of Droṇa cut them down with his sword in a fit of rage.
Having struck Uttamaujas with his feet,
he of firm prowess crushed the shouting Yudhāmanyu, who held a mace in his hand, by the throat.
Then, felling the heads of heroes to the ground with his sword,
he provided amusement for the Night of Doom as if with balls.
Without any agitation, he made the sons of Kṛṣṇa and the sons of Draupadī— who were rushing toward him—
fit prey for Time with his sword.
When the hero Prativindhya was slain, Sutasoma struck down,
Śrutakīrti, Śatānīka, and Śrutavarman were cut down.
Śikhaṇḍin, having drawn his bow, covered Droṇa’s son with arrows;
the son of Droṇa, enraged, cut him in two with his sword.
***** The Slaughter of Draupadeya and Śikhaṇḍin // 2 // ***** While being slaughtered in anger by the preceptor’s son, the Prabhadrakas,
Matsyas, Sṛñjayas, and Pāñcālas perceived Death standing close at hand. Bhājya 11.56.
Seeing him laughing, dressed in red garments, with red garlands and unguents, those heroes clearly perceived it to be the dissolution of the world.
In the thick darkness at the gate, the Bhoja and the Gautama caused the destruction of heroes— of chariots, elephants, horses, and warriors alike.
Having thus slain an akṣauhiṇī, the son of Droṇa, whose conduct was fierce and whose form was terrifying, went forth anointed with the blood of fat.
Having gone quickly together with the son of Hṛdika and Kṛpa,
he beheld King Suyodhana on the ground, his power shattered.
Repeatedly warding off the circle of flesh-eating beasts with the tip of his club,
he was tormented by a pain piercing his vital organs as he devoured the earth.
Quickly wiping away the blood flowing from his mouth,
they showered him with nectar through their account of the destruction of all the Pañcālas.
Even though his life was but a remnant, he heard this and, with his neck turned back,
praised them with indistinct words barely escaping from his lips as they were being consumed by the flames at the edges.
Embracing the son of Droṇa with effort, his eyes filled with tears, he spoke softly:
"May our reunion take place again in heaven."
Having placed his beloved upon his body and forever embracing with both arms the earth he had long enjoyed,
that hero— whose life-breath was restored by the power descending from his ear— gradually became a lover of the celestial nymphs.

***** The Ascent of Duryodhana to Heaven ***** // 3 // In the meantime, when the night had passed and their enemies were slain, the Pāṇḍavas learned of the cruel deed committed by the son of Droṇa. Bhājya 11.66.
Having heard that her sons, her younger brothers, and the Pāñcālas had been slain and liberated from that great terror, Kṛṣṇā fell to the ground in a swoon.
Gradually regaining consciousness, that beautiful-eyed woman,
lamenting and overwhelmed with grief for the sons of Pṛthā, tore their very hearts asunder.
As long as the head of the wicked son of Droṇa has not been seen by me severed by arrows, this salutation with joined palms is for my life.
Having spoken thus, Draupadī, gazing at Vṛkodara in sorrow,
said nothing more due to her anguish, having resolved upon death.
Then Bhīma, struck in his heart by the spear of grief for his beloved,
mounted his chariot and set forth with the intent to slay the son of Droṇa.
As he advanced, like the fire of time desiring to incinerate the worlds,
a frown upon his forehead momentarily created the illusion of a wreath of smoke.
"The son of Droṇa is fierce and takes refuge in Rudra, while the son of the Wind-god is enraged;
therefore, let us go behind him," Hari said to the Pāṇḍavas.
Then the sons of Pāṇḍu, led by Kirīṭin and accompanied by Sātyaki, all set forth on their chariots with arrows in hand, eager for battle.
Then, having approached the son of Droṇa, they fell into a state of agitation out of anger; he was bereft of luster and devoid of ritual action due to the sin of slaying those who were fast asleep.
When Bhīmasena was attacked while Nakula served as his charioteer, the son of Droṇa—
on foot, anointed with clarified butter on the bank of the Sarasvatī for a moment—
seized the Brahmaśīrṣa weapon in order to make the world devoid of Pāṇḍavas.
To destroy that [weapon], the skillful Pārtha also discharged the Brahmāstra,
by which the quarters were pervaded and made to tremble with waves of terror.
In the meantime, the venerable sage, the son of Satyavatī and the creator of all beings, arrived there in person along with Nārada.
Fearing the destruction of the world, he said to the son of Droṇa and to Jiṣṇu:
"In a clash of divine weapons, this one might burn the world, its heroes having been slain."
"O Pārtha, withdraw your divine weapon at my word, O son of Droṇa;
let these worlds not suffer destruction out of season."
When the sage had spoken thus, Arjuna quickly withdrew his weapon;
however, the son of Droṇa, being skilled in the employment [of weapons], was not able to withdraw his own.
Then, while the world was blazing and the host of gods was distressed,
the son of Droṇa discharged his weapon at the womb of Abhimanyu’s wife.
Furthermore, desiring a lineage of sons and wishing to counteract that [weapon],
Pārtha, provoked to anger, discharged that weapon while censuring the son of Droṇa.
Then Kṛṣṇa spoke to Jiṣṇu, who was despondent due to the extinction of his lineage:
"Do not grieve, O ocean of fortitude; your lineage shall not perish."
"By my very nature, I shall restore to life this infant son of Subhadrā, though he has been consumed by the fiery energy of the weapon, as he remains within the womb of Uttarā."
While Govinda was speaking thus and Pārtha’s weapon blazed upon the earth,
Vyāsa, together with the celestial rishi, spoke to the son of Droṇa.
Sacrifice your crest-jewel; protect the jewel of your life from this great weapon.
You are both incapable and negligent, and you do not know what is appropriate.
For a thousand years, you, afflicted with a foul disease yet composed in mind,
shall wander in solitude, miserable and appearing as a sign of famine.
Having been thus cursed, the son of the Guru spoke to Vyāsa in anger:
"Why have I, fallen into calamity, been cast by you into such a peril?"
"Wherever I may be born,
there you too shall always be my follower, O sage, by virtue of this curse."
Having spoken thus and offered his crest-jewel as a sacrificial gift for the weapon,
the son of Droṇa departed with the sage and the sage together.
Then, once the Brahmā weapon had been neutralized, the Pāṇḍavas, together with Śauri,
took the crest-jewel and presented it to Yājñasenī.
***** The Aiṣīka Weapon ***** // 4 // Having thus consoled the princess of Pañcāla, the sons of Pāṇḍu, afflicted by grief,
could find no peace as they brooded upon the terrible slaughter of the Pañcālas. Bhājana 11.93.
When Sañjaya had spoken thus, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā, having heard it,
fell for a moment unconscious from delusion, his fire of grief extinguished.
Having comforted him with showers of cool water, Saṃjaya spoke to him as he grieved for his beloved ministers and sons, his senses distressed.
Wise and steadfast men are not touched by the delusions of saṃsāra— which, like the play of dreams and illusions, ultimately bring about grief and delusion.
Those whose minds are free from intoxication are not deluded by sons, wealth, or wives, which are like the shadow-puppets created by a divine magician.
"This destruction of kinsmen was brought about by you yourself through your own misconduct;
now that it has occurred, you ought to feel grief here for no other reason than the truth."
Through states that arise from power, which are cultivated through the manifestation of illusion,
and which culminate in the ultimate realization of non-existence, no delusion is produced for the wise.
In this world sealed by its own karma, within the ocean of inevitable dissolution, I do not perceive the power of time; who indeed exists within such a vast expanse?

Thus, from the mouth of Sañjaya, they repeatedly spoke to the king— who was shattered by fierce delusion and had himself witnessed the ultimate futility of wicked policies— a discourse on the nature of worldly existence, as unstable as the swaying ears of an elephant playfully flapping its trunk.
Thus ends the Sauptika-parvan in the Bhāratamañjarī composed by Kṣemendra.
